analysis.one_liner: Strips tax breaks from Wall Street landlords, taxes their home sales at 100%, and bars federal mortgage backing for them.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in October 2024 and never received a hearing or vote, dying when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted investors with over $100 million in assets who buy single-family homes. It would take away their deductions for mortgage interest, insurance, and depreciation; charge a tax equal to the full sale price when they sell such a home; bar Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae from backing their mortgages; and send the money raised to a fund for affordable rental housing. It was introduced in the final months of the 118th Congress, referred to two committees, and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual families trying to buy a home would face less competition from giant corporate landlords, whose tax breaks and access to federally backed mortgage financing would disappear. Renters in areas dominated by investor-owned homes could benefit over time as those investors' holdings become more expensive to keep and eventually sell to families. Low-income renters gain if the new tax revenue funds affordable housing.

how_it_helps.text: Large investors would lose mortgage interest and depreciation deductions on single-family homes, removing tax advantages that help them outbid individual homebuyers.

A 100% excise tax on the sale price of any single-family home sold by a covered investor would effectively lock in those holdings and discourage further accumulation, with proceeds going to a Housing Trust Fund for affordable rental housing for extremely low- and very low-income families.

Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, and Ginnie Mae would be barred from buying, guaranteeing, or securitizing new mortgages made to covered investors, cutting off a federal financing channel for corporate homebuying.
Newly built or substantially rehabilitated homes and federally assisted housing are exempted, so the bill targets existing-home speculation rather than construction.

analysis.who_pays: Large investors (over $100 million in assets) that own single-family homes would pay through lost deductions, a 100% excise tax on home sales, and loss of Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac/Ginnie Mae financing. Some of their added costs could be passed to renters as higher rents.

drawbacks.text: The 100% excise tax on any sale could make large investors freeze their portfolios rather than sell, potentially keeping existing homes off the market instead of returning them to families.

By stripping deductions and financing access, the bill raises large investors' cost of holding homes, which some economists warn could be passed through to renters as higher rents, at least until new supply is built.
The bill targets only investors with over $100 million in assets, leaving smaller corporate landlords and individual investor-owners untouched.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main drawbacks are design risk: a 100% excise tax on sales could make large investors reluctant to sell homes at all, which would not add a single house to the market, and raising big landlords' costs could pass through to rents in the short run before new supply responds. It also does nothing about the many small and mid-sized landlords contributing to the problem. On the other side, it attacks the specific financing advantages that let giant investors outbid families for starter homes, funds affordable housing with the proceeds, and exempts new construction and federally assisted housing. The benefits plausibly outweigh the costs, though the harshness of the exit tax is a real design question.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees the day it was introduced and no committee ever acted on it before the 118th Congress ended, so it never came to a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on October 22, 2024, with 10 original cosponsors, late in the second session of the 118th Congress.
It was referred to the Ways and Means and Financial Services Committees, neither of which held a markup or reported it out.
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, and the bill died with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporate landlords keep their tax deductions, their access to federally backed mortgage financing, and their freedom to sell homes without an exit tax. Individual homebuyers competing against them gain nothing.

for.name: Original cosponsors (Porter, Takano, Grijalva, Frost, Cherfilus-McCormick, Watson Coleman, Jackson of Illinois, Deluzio, Lee of CA)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; 11 total cosponsors, all Democrats.

against.name: Single-family rental industry (e.g., Invitation Homes, American Homes 4 Rent and allied lobbying)
against.what_they_did: The major corporate landlords the bill targeted have historically lobbied and contributed against restrictions on investor homebuying; no opposition from them appears in the congressional record, but their stake in the bill's death was direct.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled House never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Large corporate single-family rental investors (over $100M in assets)
industries.note: The bill would strip their tax deductions on single-family homes, tax their home sales at 100% of the sale price, and cut off Fannie/Freddie/Ginnie financing. This is the industry the bill was written to shrink.

industries.industry: Mortgage finance and securitization industry serving large landlords
industries.note: Lenders and securitizers that package loans for big single-family rental owners would lose a federally backed channel of business.

New construction and substantial rehabilitation are exempt from the deductions ban and exit tax, so building homes remains favored over buying existing ones; homebuilders are largely spared, and new supply is a public benefit.
